FIRST(A): look at the START of each production of A. A terminal goes straight in; a nonterminal → copy its FIRST (and, if it can vanish, look at the next one).
FOLLOW: look for A on the RIGHT SIDE of the productions and see what comes right after. The start symbol always has $. If A is at the end, it inherits the FOLLOW of the left side.

For each item with • before a NONTERMINAL B, add B → •γ for EVERY production of B. Repeat for the new items!
Items with the • in the middle (like X → a • b) are never added by the closure.

Some cells of the SLR table are hidden (?). Tap the ones with a CONFLICT (two actions).
Shift/reduce conflict: the state has an item A → α • (reduce) AND an item with • before the terminal t, with t ∈ FOLLOW(A).
You got %1$s% of the hidden cells right. Real conflicts:
With %left '+' and then %left '*' (the * binds tighter), what does Bison do in state %1$s seeing '%2$s'? (complete item: %3$s)
We compare the precedence of the token '%1$s' with the rule's (its last terminal).
The rule is stronger, or equal with %left → REDUCE.
Without declaring precedence, how does Bison resolve the 'dangling else'?
SHIFT: the else goes with the nearest if
REDUCE: the else goes with the outer if
By default, Bison prefers SHIFT (and reports the conflict). That attaches the else to the innermost if, exactly what C and Java do.
This conflict exists in SLR because FOLLOW(R) contains '='. And in LALR(1)?
It's gone: the lookahead of the item R → L• in that state is just $
LALR uses specific lookaheads per state, more precise than the global FOLLOW. That's why Bison (LALR) accepts this grammar.
This grammar has no SLR conflicts. That means…
it's not ambiguous (SLR grammars are never ambiguous)
Every LR grammar (with no conflicts) is unambiguous. But it may NOT be LL(1); this one has left recursion!
Bison's golden rule: in a conflict, it compares the precedence of the incoming TOKEN with the RULE's (given by the rule's last terminal).

🏭 Drag the phases onto the CONVEYOR in the order the code goes through them:
First the text becomes tokens, then the tokens become a tree. Only after that can you check types.
Optimization comes after intermediate code and before the final code.
Pipeline built! Lexical → Syntactic → Semantic → Intermediate → Optimization → Code.
'@' doesn't belong to any token pattern: the scanner doesn't even know what it is.
The string never closes its quotes: the lexical phase can't form the string token.
'#' is an invalid character in the language: lexical error.
All tokens are valid, but an operand is missing after '>': the STRUCTURE is wrong.
The parentheses required by the while grammar are missing.
A parenthesis opened and never closed: only a grammar (not a regex) notices that.
A ';' is missing between the declarations: the token sequence doesn't match any rule.
The sentence is well-formed, but assigning a string to an int breaks the TYPE rules.
Perfect syntax; but the symbol table has no 'z': semantic error.
Declaring the same name twice in the same scope: semantic.
f(1, 2); // f was declared with 1 parameter
Wrong number of arguments: semantic check.
In C the compiler usually doesn't know the index at compile time: it blows up at runtime.
Division by zero with values that only exist when the program runs: runtime error.
'whille' becomes an IDENTIFIER (it's not a keyword!) and 'whille(x)' looks like a call to an undeclared function: semantic. The lexical phase has no way to know it was a typo.
The scanner produces NUM(2) and ID(x), valid tokens! But 'int NUM ID' doesn't match the declaration rule: syntactic.
Lexical = impossible character/word. Syntactic = tokens OK but wrong structure. Semantic = structure OK but wrong meaning (types, declarations). Runtime = depends on real values.

Longest match rule: the scanner swallows the LONGEST possible lexeme. `>=` is ONE token; `count2` is ONE identifier.
Words like `iff` or `whilex` are NOT keywords: they're identifiers!

🚨 At which token does the LL(1) parser NOTICE the error?
LL(1) reads from left to right and stops at the FIRST token that no valid sentence could have in that position.
In panic mode, the parser throws tokens away until it finds a sync token (a token in the nonterminal's FOLLOW, like ';').
The error is detected at '%1$s' (token %2$s). Viable prefix property: everything before it could still be a valid program.
Now **panic mode**: tap the token where the parser GETS BACK to normal work (the sync token).
Instead of stopping at the first error, the compiler recovers and keeps going; that way it lists ALL the errors in a single compilation.

**Step 1: liveness:** mark which temporaries are ALIVE right AFTER each instruction (they'll still be used further down).
Work from the BOTTOM UP: after the last instruction nothing is alive.
in = use ∪ (out − def): a temporary stays alive from where it's defined until its last use.
**Step 2: coloring:** use only **%1$s** register(s). Tap a temporary and then a register. Neighbors (alive together) can't share a register!
Start with the node with the MOST neighbors. Nodes with no edge between them can reuse a register.
%1$s conflict(s): temporaries alive at the same time sharing a register.

The Compilers course project asks for a whole compiler: a scanner with automata, an LL(1) grammar, recursive descent, a symbol table, types and MIPS assembly generation. This guide walks through each step with an example language.

A network with **10 inputs → 12 neurons → 1 output** runs on your phone and gets trained after every match.
It looks at your estimated mastery (BKT), how much you remember (forgetting curve), recent hits, challenge level and your confidence, and predicts your chance of getting it right.
The game uses this to pick challenges around a ~75% chance: hard enough to teach, doable enough not to frustrate.
